stat_summary: Men in England travel 6,549 miles a year on average, compared with 5,633 for women, but make fewer trips (904 against 939). Men also make 125 commuting trips a year against 98 for women, and 80% of men hold a full driving licence compared with 71% of women.
stat_source_title: National Travel Survey 2024, Department for Transport

male.headline: Road Warriors: Men Cover 916 Extra Miles a Year While Society Looks the Other Way
male.standfirst: New government figures confirm what every bloke stuck on the M25 already knew: men are doing the heavy lifting on Britain's roads, and getting precisely zero thanks for it.
male.image_caption: Gary, 47, somewhere on the M25, with the wardrobe.
body_paragraphs: New government figures have confirmed what every bloke already knows from the hard shoulder of the M25: men are doing the heavy lifting on Britain's roads. The average man now clocks up 6,549 miles a year – a thumping 916 more than the average woman – and receives, in return, precisely zero thanks.
“I drove to Leeds and back for a single flat-pack wardrobe,” said Gary, 47, from Swindon. “Nobody threw me a parade. Nobody even offered me a Ginsters.”

The same official survey shows men making 125 commuting trips a year, against 98 for women. That means more traffic jams, more tolls, and more time listening to a podcast they stopped enjoying in 2019. Campaigners are already calling for a national Mileage Recognition Day, and for a dedicated lane on every motorway reserved for men who are, in their words, “just trying to get there”.
Yet where is the outrage? Where is the prime-time documentary? Britain's silent long-distance hero motors on, alone, with only his sat-nav for company.
male.pull_quote: Nobody threw me a parade. Nobody even offered me a Ginsters.

female.headline: Death by a Thousand Errands: Women Make More Trips Than Men, and Experts Say It's No Coincidence
female.standfirst: Official statistics have finally exposed the hidden logistics crisis gripping British women, and it does not look anything like a Sunday drive.
body_paragraphs: Official statistics have at last exposed the hidden logistics crisis gripping British women. Women make 939 trips a year – 35 more than men – zig-zagging between school gates, pharmacies, birthday parties and the one Tesco that still stocks the right yoghurt.
“He does one big drive to Leeds and acts like he's crossed the Sahara,” said Claire, 44, also from Swindon. “I did eleven stops before 9am and nobody's called me a road warrior.”

Researchers note that men's longer journeys are often simple A-to-B affairs, while women's are tactical multi-stop missions requiring the planning skills of a NATO general. Meanwhile, just 71 per cent of women hold a full driving licence, compared with 80 per cent of men, meaning a good many of those trips involve buses, lifts and sheer willpower.

Campaigners are demanding a Trip Equality Act and a national apology for the phrase “while you're out, can you just…”. Until then, the country's unofficial logistics corps will keep moving, one forgotten birthday card at a time.
female.pull_quote: I did eleven stops before 9am and nobody's called me a road warrior.
